pages.text:
*From the Dropout Club Handbook, Rule 11: If everyone suddenly turns into a gnome, stay calm and take notes.*

The Great Hall was silent, except for the sound of hundreds of tiny feet waddling. The students sat in neat rows, their bright blue jackets shiny, their red hats perfectly straight. They were all smiling. Every single one of them had the same cheerful, painted smile, fixed in place as if they had just won a prize they didn’t understand. A tray of tiny cakes slid off the hand of the Head Boy, shattering into a glittering pile of crumbs.

In the front row, a very short figure with a brass hat that covered his entire head was trying to lift his tuba, which was now the size of a dinner plate. He looked confused. He looked happy. He looked exactly like a garden gnome that had wandered into a music lesson.

Marnie stared. She looked at Toby, who was pushing up his glasses with one finger. Lulu was tugging at her sleeve, looking terrified. Bunt stood in the doorway, his enormous boots taking up half the floor, and he sniffed the air. His nose twitched.

Gerald, the goose, landed on the stage. He honked once, a loud, satisfied sound, and settled his purple ribbon. He seemed to think this was the best day of his life.
pages.image: A chaotic scene in a grand wizard hall with hundreds of tiny two-foot-tall garden gnomes with red hats and blue jackets sitting in rows; Gerald with a purple ribbon stands on the stage looking pleased, while a large troll in a brown vest stands in the doorway.

pages.text:
Toby pulled a small notebook from his pocket. He wrote down: *Observation 1: They are alive. Observation 2: They cannot cast spells.* He tested this by waving his wand at a gnome. Nothing happened. The gnome did not even blink. It just smiled its fixed smile and waddled a step to the left.

Cassius Pomeroy was on the stage. He was no taller than a teacup. His golden hair stuck out from under his red pointed hat like a stiff brush. He held his silver wand, but it was so long it looked like a pike. He stared at it with an expression of pure, unadulterated horror.

"How?" he squeaked. His voice was very small. "I am perfect."

Marnie flinched at the word. It sounded like a crack in a plate. Cassius looked at his hands, then at his wand, then at the sky. He tried to cast a spell. A small puff of air came out. He went pale. His lower lip began to tremble. He looked ready to cry, but he had no tears.

Toby wrote: *Observation 3: Cassius is upset. This is irregular.*
pages.image: A tiny garden gnome version of Cassius with golden hair sticking out from a red hat stands on a stage holding a wand that is far too long for his hands, looking shocked, while a large boy with round glasses watches from the side.

pages.text:
"Fix it," the Principal-gnome squeaked. He was standing on a stack of tiny chairs. His moustache was standing straight up, defying gravity, like two stiff whiskers. "This is highly irregular. I demand a solution. Immediately."

Marnie took a step forward. Her heart was beating in her throat. She raised her wand, her hand shaking. "Straighten!" she whispered.

There was a puff of grey smoke. The Principal’s wand, which he had been holding stiffly, turned into a sausage. A very good-looking sausage. It fell to the floor with a soft *thud*. The Principal-gnome stared at it. His painted smile did not change.

Toby stepped in. "Backwards, Gnome!" he said.

For one second, the Principal-gnome grew two inches tall. Then, with a pop, he shrank back down. He looked at Toby with wide, surprised eyes. It was the first real expression anyone had seen on a gnome face.
pages.image: The Principal-gnome, a two-foot-tall garden gnome with a long white moustache and a purple robe with silver stars, stands on a stack of tiny chairs staring at a sausage on the floor, while Marnie and Toby look on in panic.

pages.text:
Suddenly, a flying carpet zoomed through the windows, trailing silk ribbons that whipped around the chandeliers. Two men in grey suits landed on the stage, looking like accountants who had wandered into a very colorful dream. They scanned the room with cold, sharp eyes, checking for anything out of place.

"A minor incident," one said, raising his wand with a snap. "Restore!"

The spell hit the air, clean and precise, exactly right. A wave of gold glitter rippled out from his wand, catching the dust motes before they could settle. It struck the second inspector before he could blink.

The second man froze. A red hat popped onto his head, fitting as snugly as a lid on a jar. He became a gnome, complete with a bright blue jacket and a smile that looked painted on.

The first inspector looked at his hands, then at his friend, and finally up at the ceiling. His mouth opened, but no sound came out. He tried to cast another spell, but the air shimmered, and a red hat popped onto his head too.

Toby’s pencil stopped moving. He watched the two new gnomes waddle in place, their little feet clicking on the wooden stage. "It feeds on perfection," he said quietly. "The more perfect the spell, the more it spreads."
pages.image: Two men in grey suits standing on a flying carpet, one of whom is turning into a garden gnome with a red hat while golden glitter swirls in the air, while a boy with glasses watches with a notebook.

pages.text:
A huge golden clock appeared on the wall of the Great Hall. It had no numbers, only a single hand that began to move, slowly, toward the top. The face of the clock ticked with a sound like a heavy drop of honey falling.

Seventy-two hours. That was how long they had before the gnomes became permanent. Before the school, the village, perhaps the whole world, became a garden of smiling, blue-jacketed statues.

The golden wave was spreading out the doors now, rolling across the lawn like a slow tide of light. It touched the stone steps, and the stones shimmered. It touched the hedge, and the leaves turned bright, perfect green.

Marnie felt very small. She looked at the clock, then at the gnomes, then at her friends. Her voice was very quiet. "We need a plan."

Toby closed his notebook. He looked at Bunt, who was reaching for a biscuit tin that was the size of a bathtub. "We need a great deal of biscuits," Toby said.

Bunt did not answer. He was already pouring tea from a kettle that had appeared out of nowhere. He looked, for the first time, very calm.
pages.image: A large golden clock on a stone wall with a single moving hand, while a girl with copper-red hair and a boy with glasses look up at it; in the background, a troll pours tea from a large kettle near a pile of biscuits.
